In our research, we develop new families of holographic error correction codes, based on a modified version of the existing MERLin code, which we find can be characterized by their behavior under the holographic property. This leads us to introduce a new concept, hyper-invariance, which enables the use of a single parameter to define both the structure and capacity of these codes at different scales. The parametric dependence on system size is common in various many-body systems, and our findings indicate that hyper-invariance offers an effective framework for designing and analyzing holographic quantum error correction codes. Through simulations on a specific type of quantum error correction code, implemented using the holographic quantum surface code, our results show that hyper-invariance can effectively describe both the structure and capacity of these codes, even in cases where the parametric dependence on system size is quite pronounced. Additionally, our analysis highlights the importance of considering system size in the design of these codes, which significantly impacts their capacity for correction. The concept of hyper-invariance provides a valuable tool for understanding and optimizing the performance of these codes, and our research offers a new direction for developing efficient QECs for quantum computers with large, extended quantum systems. The approximation of hyper-invariance allows us to design efficient HQECs that achieve optimal error thresholds at large scales, which is crucial for the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Current text generation algorithms typically fall short when confronted with basic requirements for human-like communication. To address this, our research introduces a new framework that enables end-to-end text production guided by linguistic rules. By incorporating surface-level constraints, this model learns to generate coherent and grammatically correct text, even in complex dialogue situations. Our results demonstrate substantial improvements over the existing state-of-the-art, setting a new standard in text production. Furthermore, our framework outperforms other reference models, including GPT-2, in various evaluation metrics. Our findings suggest that rule-based surface-level constraints are essential for text layout, whereas higher-level principles are essential for dialogue meaning. This separation of concerns not only boosts text quality but also accelerates training efficiency. Using our framework on a particular dataset, we achieved high-quality results within three iterations. To facilitate future research, we publicly release our framework and associated materials at https://github.com/google-research/leather. To fill this gap, researchers turn to laboratory and wind-tunnel tests, but with limited field measurements, it becomes difficult to validate computational models that aim to predict wind-turbine lifespan. We demonstrate that a particular class of groups, including generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups and some nilpotent groups, possess property $R_\infty$.  This result is a direct consequence of a more general theorem regarding the isomorphism between group quotients and nilpotent groups, and can be visualized as a generalized version of the correspondence between lattices and tori. There is an ongoing, yet inconclusive debate among researchers about the predominant mechanism driving intelligence in neural systems. Some scientists support the representation approach, attributing intelligence to neural representations of patterns, whether it be in images, words, or numbers. Conversely, others advocate for the processing perspective, suggesting intelligence arises from reconfiguring and manipulating neural data. To resolve this dispute, we examined the representation and processing methods utilized in three neural networks, trained on three distinct neural tasks. Our findings indicate that the systems represent numbers, words, and spatial patterns differently but also process and manipulate underlying neural data when performing these tasks. This discovery leads us to conclude that the coexistence of representation and processing approaches is necessary to fully comprehend the nature of intelligence in neural systems. This work has implications for developing future artificial neural systems and contributes insights towards a deeper understanding of the human brain's functioning. Furthermore, our research also sheds light on the potential similarities and differences between artificial and human neural systems, highlighting the significance of representation and processing in neural cognition. This study is part of a larger project, "Understanding Common and Deep Distinctions between Human and Artificial Neural Cognition," aiming to investigate the essential components of neural intelligence. Inspired by the question "What is one thing that neural networks are better at than humans?" and "What is one thing that humans are better at than neural networks?" posed by the Distinguished Researcher, Dr. Yujin Y. Song from MIT, this work seeks to elucidate the fundamental aspects of neural intelligence. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating C code and validating its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 code. The tool embeds C code in a shallow representation within ACL2 and utilizes a series of reduction rules to facilitate reduction and reasoning. By manually crafting each reduction rule, it preserves C's semantic essence and the overall translation remains efficient. The proposed approach is distinct from traditional state-transformation based embedding methods, offering a more streamlined and coherent approach. Our evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of this technique, with the generated proofs exceeding the limit of the standard ACL2 stack size only marginally, roughly 10-20% on average. This method was successfully applied to a real-world project involving the ACL2-flavored microkernels development for an embedded hardware platform's firmware. This study investigates how grammatical gender influences the representation of nouns in languages that indicate gender. We utilized word2vec on a French and Spanish corpus, examining the impact of artificial additions of 'feminine' and'masculine' markers on the embedded meaning representations of nouns. We found that these markers affect the embedded representation of nouns significantly, and the direction of the influence aligns with cultural and societal gender classifications, defying expectations of neutrality. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the associations captured by word2vec include intricate aspects of human culture. Building upon these results, we initiated a sequence of automatic ethical considerations for machine learning systems. These considerations center around the potential perpetuation of existing social biases within the design of AI. We propose a framework for detecting and mitigating biases in machine representations, outlining strategies for identifying and addressing these issues through generalization, reversal, and expansion. The presented research highlights the need for further investigation into the social and cultural impact of language models, promoting reflection on the ethical implications of automated intelligence. We hope that this study serves as a foundation for future research in this area. Our results address charmability in a weighted Hilbert space context and under the assumption of a stiffness condition. Our characterizations for arithmetic groups imply that only finitely many representations satisfy the stiffness condition. Additionally, we provide a concrete description of stiff representations for SL(2, R), highlighting instances of infinitely many stiff representations. Furthermore, we prove the stiffness of all proper arithmetic group representations with a charactrizer rank of two or more. Our study also explores applications to the spectral gap problem, showing that representations with a large charactrizer rank contribute significantly to the one-way gain. Our results further imply that representations with a charactrizer rank of 5 or more yield a one-way gain of at least a constant multiple of the Margulis constant. Finally, we prove that representations with a large charactrizer rank lead to a finite number of elements with a semi-stable orbit in the character spectrum for any infinite-dimensional representation of a finite volume hyperbolic manifold. A growing trend within CPS is the distributed network of Cyber-Physical Systems, often referred to as cyber-physical networks. This research combines concepts from control theory and computer science to explore CPS interconnection, presenting a framework for designing CPS with intelligence. A formal representation of CPS relationships is established through the use of digraphs and matrix representations. Studies have shown that, given certain parameters, a CPN can be considered stable under specific conditions, and have developed an algorithm to test these conditions. Notably, research has found that, under certain circumstances, a stable CPN can remain stable even when individual CPS remain stable, providing insights into CPS behavior. This research has potential applications in various cyber-physical networks, including the control of traffic flow and management of factory production. Ultimately, this research aims to demystify CPS behavior and CPN dynamics, providing a foundation for designing intelligent cyber-physical networks. The authors present a new perspective on CPS and CPN analysis, drawing from past work in control theory and computer science. A major challenge in information retrieval research remains developing effective models that can be both efficient and scalable.  From a theoretical standpoint, independent indexing models provide efficiency and scalability, but they struggle with matching quality.  On the other hand, interactive models excel in matching quality, but they fall short on efficiency and scalability.  This paper investigates the potential benefits of combining the strengths of both types of models to improve cross-lingual information retrieval.  By integrating a fast, non-interactive model to pre-filter documents and applying relevance feedback to re-rank results within an interactive model, the overall system can balance high matching quality with improved efficiency and scalability.  Experimental results demonstrate that this hybrid approach leads to significant gains in average retrieval precision and scalability without sacrificing too much in terms of efficiency compared to using solely interactive models.  Moreover, using a combined score of non-interactive and interactive models as the ranking score also yields substantial improvements in average retrieval precision and scalability.  Experiments conducted with 10 monolingual data streams and 20 cross-lingual collections show that this hybrid model is well-suited for handling various sub-scenarios such as handling a large number of queries, handling a large number of documents, and handling an extensive number of cross-lingual collections.  Finally, the hybrid model outperforms traditional information retrieval techniques widely used as the standard in the field, such as BM25.  From a practical standpoint, the hybrid model enables a system to efficiently and effectively handle a large number of queries concurrently, for example up to 1 million queries at a time in a production environment.  Such capabilities make the hybrid model an attractive candidate for large-scale cross-lingual information retrieval applications.  Our model is available for public use at https://github.com/krishnarajendrakr/CLIR.  From a research perspective, the hybrid model opens up new possibilities for leveraging the strengths of different models to improve retrieval performance and is available at https://www.dropbox.com/s/3m8m9gkq5kq5kq5/CLIR-models.zip.  Researchers can use this model by simply uploading the model parameters, which provide state-of-the-art retrieval performance, and are available through a simple http upload. In low- and middle-income countries, detailed information about health and wellness is often estimated using small-area modeling techniques, particularly given the limited availability of survey and census data. This research compares the performance of three potential approaches for modeling survey data: design-based estimators using pseudo-weights, model-based estimators using simulated weights, and model-based estimators with fitted weights. The analysis uses real-world survey data from Tanzania as a case study. This investigation looks at three key scenarios, assessing how the methods perform when there are varying levels of undercoverage and misclassification. The results indicate that model-based estimators with fitted weights yield more precise results in scenarios with misclassification, but design-based estimators with pseudo-weights are more suitable for scenarios with undercoverage. This is largely due to pseudo-weights being less sensitive to model fit. Combining the strengths of both approaches through the use of pseudo-weights for undercoverage scenarios and fitting weights for misclassification scenarios is proposed as a potential solution. This method allows for the calculation of pseudo-weights using summary data and can be applied to any model. This has the advantage of not requiring users to models for estimating survey data. This research also addresses other limitations associated with model-based estimators, providing recommendations for their improvement. Ultimately, this research aims to improve small-area estimation methods for health and wellness outcomes in low- and middle-income countries. We explore the problem of creating control policies for complex tasks using machine learning. Traditional approaches often train models using vast amounts of data, but we instead focus on scenarios where data is scarce and noisy. By treating control as a problem influenced by dynamics, we develop models that capture task-related patterns despite lacking comprehensive knowledge of the underlying system. This is achieved by incorporating task-specific information and by selecting informative data points for training. We introduce two new methods: one method creates task-related dynamics models using a variety of general information sources, while the other method develops models specifically tailored to each task. Both methods allow us to transfer knowledge across related tasks, even when no data is available. We demonstrate these methods in simulated environments, including reaching, flying, walking, and swimming. Additionally, we show that they can also be applied in real-world robotics control. These methods are available online at https://github.com/andreab Rossi SID.\\

We present Relation GAN, a novel architecture that enhances training stability and effectiveness in generator discriminators through relational information. Leveraging relation networks, relation GAN combines triplet loss to facilitate direct and indirect discrimination of real and fake images. Triplet loss within relation GAN promotes more nuanced discrimination by minimizing the similarity between negative images, whether they share the same input, differ in inputs, or have disparate feature maps. Furthermore, triplet loss allows for flexible selection of training criteria, enabling the development of custom loss functions. Consequently, relation GAN exhibits superior performance and enhanced training stability, outperforming state-of-the-art discriminators, including those utilizing activation normalization, as evidenced by experiments with Cycle GAN and CIFAR-10. The corresponding source code can be found at https://github.com/wwhher/Relation-GAN. In addition, our study reveals that certain existing normalized discriminators, deemed superior by other researchers, demonstrate inferior performance in our investigation. Therefore, we highlight the importance of method scrutiny and rigorous testing before claiming state-of-the-art achievements in deep learning research. Our analysis also shows that a well-designed discriminator with improved stability does not always translate to higher fidelity output generation; rather, it may result in minimal gains. Object identification, a critical component of many applications, typically requires extensive labor and time to create a comprehensive dataset. Conventional techniques rely on closed vocabulary, where they can only use a fixed set of known object categories. In contrast, open vocabulary object identification allows for the detection and identification of any object, regardless of whether it is included in the pre-defined list or not. However, it typically requires even more labor and time to gather data, as each sample needs to be manually labeled by experts. This paper proposes an innovative method to obtain pseudo labels for the open vocabulary object identification task. These pseudo labels are then used to train a model that can accurately identify objects. While the pseudo labels may contain some errors, we have found that as the number of original labels increases, our proposed method can outperform other state-of-the-art models that also use pseudo labels to guide their training. We have tested our approach on multiple datasets and the results show that it is highly effective. For instance, when there are only a handful of original labels available (20 or 100), our proposed method can outperform a state-of-the-art baseline that also uses pseudo labels by a significant margin, with a performance gap of up to 8% or better. Furthermore, when there are more original labels available (500 or 2500), our proposed method can outperform a state-of-the-art baseline that also uses pseudo labels with an even more significant margin, with a performance gap of up to 10% or better. These results show that our proposed method is highly effective in guiding the training of an open vocabulary object identification model. We have also found that one key factor contributes to the success of our proposed method, which is the quality of the pseudo labels themselves. By refining the pseudo labels to reduce errors and improve accuracy, our proposed method can outperform a state-of-the-art baseline that also uses pseudo labels even further, with a performance gap of up to 12% or better. These results show that the quality of the pseudo labels is a critical factor that can affect the performance of our proposed method. Lastly, our proposed method is not limited to the open vocabulary object identification task and can be extended to other computer vision tasks, where pseudo labels can guide their training to achieve state-of-the-art performance. For instance, when we applied our proposed method to the image segmentation task, we found that it performed exceptionally well, with a performance gap of up to 30% or better from the state-of-the-art baseline that also uses pseudo labels to guide their training. This study delves into the limitations of current neural architecture search (NAS) methods, which often yield similar architectures due to weak mitigation of bias in their design. A thorough examination of the bias-generating factors is conducted, followed by the development of a novel, bias-reduction technique, which employs (relatively) uniform sampling across the NAS's search space to produce diverse architectures. To facilitate this, a 'randomized DNN search' method is introduced that allows for (relatively uniform) exploration of the NAS's search space. Moreover, a theoretical explanation of the NAS's bias is provided, showing that NAS's bias arises from (relatively) uniform sampling in the search space. Experimental results validate the proposed technique, which not only reduces NAS's bias but also (significantly) improves the resulting model's performance and (considerably) shortens the search time required. Notably, when employing the proposed technique on the ResNet and DenseNet models, the resulting top model surpasses the top model obtained from the renowned AutoML system, Google AutoML, by (significant) 1.0 and (considerable) 0.7 percentage points, respectively. A corresponding source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jejelee95/bias-reduction-nas. Furthermore, a high-level guide on how to reduce NAS's bias effectively is presented below. \begin{enumerate} \item Ensure that the search space is not overly constrained. \item Employ (relatively) uniform sampling. \item Increase the degree of diversity in the search space. \item Reduce over-reliance on biased factors. \item Use diverse learning objectives. \item Use transfer learning. \end{enumerate} Such strategies can (significantly) help to mitigate NAS's bias and (considerably) improve the resulting model's performance. \end{abstract}

We focus on the problem of optimizing the value of a lottery ticket in a dynamic market. A lottery ticket consists of a set of properties and their associated probabilities. The total value of the ticket is calculated by multiplying each property's value by its corresponding probability and summing the results. Our objective is to maximize the total value by strategically buying and selling properties over discrete time periods.

The outcome of each property at any given time is uncertain and follows a binary distribution with two possible states: success with a given probability p or failure. Properties evolve independently according to Markov dynamics. At the beginning of each time step, the current state of each property is revealed, and a ticket owner can choose to sell or keep the property for the next time step. This decision-making process repeats for a specified number of time steps.

Theoretical analysis shows that this policy achieves results comparable to the optimal solution in scenarios with a limited number of properties and known property values. The primary goal of existing lidar-camera fusion techniques is to enhance the representation capacity of detection models for objects in both lidar and camera spaces. However, conventional methods employ two-way fusion, which often complicates the process and leads to over-reliance on pre-existing pointclouds. Furthermore, they frequently neglect to capture direct spatial relationships between objects in the two different sensory modalities. To address these limitations, we introduce a simple yet efficient lidar-camera fusion framework known as BEVFusion, which treats them as separate beams within a unified volumetric representation. This novel approach enables efficient and memory-friendly fusion by leveraging beam-to-beam spatial correlation to build a cohesive understanding of objects in both lidar and camera spaces. As a result, our framework outperforms existing methods by achieving consistent improvements across various experiments. Notably, we have achieved state-of-the-art performance on nuScenes benchmark and achieved a 4 m AP gain compared to the previous best result. The code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuangul/BEVFusion.

Historically, partner particles associated with gluons have been most easily accessible through single production processes, but more recently, researchers have begun exploring single production methods for partners linked to other fundamental gauge bosons.  In this study, a non-resonant top and bottom partner production process is proposed, supplementing existing resonance production methods and potentially offering significant advantages in simulation analysis and interpretation.  By extending electroweak symmetry, partner particles can easily exceed masses of 1 TeV, allowing for their potential detection in experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).  Traditional searches for these partner particles have focused on resonant production methods, but the proposed non-resonant approach may provide a more effective detection strategy, given the absence of theoretical limitations.  In this study, single production of these partner particles is modeled using standard model effective field theory and a simplified model, with simulations conducted of potential detections at LHC runs 2 and 3.  Results show that with sufficient luminosity and energy in experiments at LHC, non-resonant detection methods of these partner particles may be more sensitive than traditional resonance detection methods. The rise of portable imaging devices has made it possible to capture visual data sequences cost-effectively and efficiently, even in environments where storage is limited and expensive. To address this issue and recover complete visual data from devices, we can use learning-based methods that leverage data prediction. One specific method, streaming tensor loop completion, utilizes 3D predictive modeling to recover missing data, but it requires a continuous input sequence and a pre-trained model. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new approach called patch tracking-based streaming tensor loop completion, which uses patch tracking to continuously update the input sequence and maintain the continuity of 3D predictive models. Moreover, our approach can utilize a dynamic graph to adaptively select features from the patch sequence for prediction. By evaluating our method and comparing it with existing techniques, we have achieved promising results on real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential applications in practical scenarios, including image and video compression, and lossless image and video transmission. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold: (1) we have proposed a novel method that can perform 3D predictive modeling without relying on pre-trained models or continuous sequences; (2) our approach is efficient and scalable, requiring only a small context window and previous patch sequence to update features and models dynamically; (3) we have successfully applied our method to recover complete visual data from devices, and our results indicate that our approach is more effective and efficient than existing techniques, including a streaming method that utilizes 3D predictive modeling. Notably, our method has achieved comparable results with existing methods on real-world datasets, and our results suggest that our approach is more effective and efficient than existing techniques. The long-term numerical simulation of turbulent wave spectra reveals an unusual pattern where the variance of certain wave modes exhibits a distinctive 3/2 power-law pattern when considering modes of sufficient intensity. This behavior supports the theory that a collision between waves produces a specific spectrum, known as the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. Although our simulation confirms the existence of this spectrum in turbulent wave energy and conservative quantities like enstrophy, it shows that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum does not apply to other properties like angular momentum. The presence of resonant interactions with external forces causes fluctuations in conservative quantities like angular momentum to deviate from the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum pattern. On the other hand, non-conservative quantities like momentum do not follow this spectrum due to the continuous transfer of momentum from wave modes to a mean flow. Finally, extending the theory of wave turbulence to include interactions between waves and mean flows shows that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum should not appear in non-conservative quantities like momentum. These findings support the idea that the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum is a reliable indicator of true turbulent behavior. The theoretical basis for our conclusions is rooted in the renormalized perturbation theory of wave-turbulence. The applicability of this theory to real-world oceanic turbulence remains an open question. The existence of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum in our simulation suggests that the renormalized perturbation theory provides an accurate description of oceanic turbulence. We investigate a novel problem known as Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN). The objective of IGN is to continuously remove edges with the lowest weights from a graph until no more edges can be eliminated. The problem of interest has emerged within the context of finding maximum weight independent sets in graphs. Through theoretical analysis, we establish a lower bound limit of 1/np (where n is the number of vertices and p is the edge participation ratio) on the normalization factor F(1/p) for graphs with girth g, which also reveals that this limit can be approached asymptotically as p → 0. The findings of our study contribute a theoretical basis for understanding graph normalization in the realm of graph theory and related discourses. The work presented here diverges from standard discussions by considering participation ratio p as the primary parameter of interest instead of other customary parameters like the graph's size or a fixed constant. The results of our investigation also shed light on the rate of convergence to the limit by showing that the normalization factor F(δ) for a graph is less than e^(1/(2*sqrt(δ))) for certain situations. Based on these theoretical analysis results, we further investigate IGN on random graphs with the PA2 model participation distribution and evaluate the effect of the participation ratio on the graph's sparsity. The results of our study also suggest that the participation distribution plays a crucial role in determining the efficiency of the iterative normalization process. Our research focuses on the computational study of trimer-based quantum magnets arranged in a two-dimensional lattice structure. Specifically, we examined a model lattice pattern featuring 2D arrays of three-spin clusters connected by weak interactions. We employed cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations to generate phase diagrams for two variations of this model, which differ in their use of nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) and next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) interactions. Our findings suggest that the model lattice pattern with $J_1 = 1$ and $J_2 = 0.125$ exhibits antiferromagnetic long-range order below the critical temperature $T_N \approx 0.119(3)$. We discovered that the critical temperature for larger cluster sizes is consistent with previous computational studies and increases slightly with the size of the clusters. However, the method used to compute the energy for smaller cluster sizes may have contributed to a discrepancy with previous research, which found no long-range order above a certain temperature ($T^* \approx 0.129$) in the model lattice pattern with $J_1 = 1$ and $J_2 = 0.125$). Our analysis indicates that the model is likely paramagnetic above this temperature ($T^*$) and the lack of long-range order in this region is not due to computational limitations. This dissertation examines the statistical analysis of nonparametric estimations of the conditional expectation operator given by $M_{F}(X)$, where the conditional expectation $F$ is perturbed by observations of a random sample $(X_i, Y_i)$ drawn from $(X, Y)$ with $X$ defined as a Banach space-valued random variable and Y is a real-valued random variable. The estimations $M_F^*(X)$ of $M_F(X)$ are derived using either linear or nonlinear regression-type estimators, where the regressor space is a subset of the Banach space over the $\ell_p$-space for $1 \leq p < \infty$. The study explores convergence rates, where the rates of convergence are influenced by the smoothness of the conditional expectation $F$ and the smoothness of the conditional marginal distribution of $X$. It also investigates the effects of dimensionality by comparing the rates of convergence under different types of regressor spaces. The findings are further supported by numerical simulations in medical and work-in-progress related fields. The statistical results are shown to be applicable in a Hilbert space context as demonstrated in a recent study by Cai, Cai and Kang (2020). The estimators $M_F^*(X)$ are evaluated in a least-squares framework, where the bias and variance of the estimators $M_F^*(X)$ are analyzed. The study also derives finite sample convergence rates for $M_F^*(X)$ with a minimum sample size requirement for the estimators to converge. The findings are further extended to derive pointwise central limit theorems for the estimators $M_F^*(X)$. The results of the statistical analysis are applied in two estimators $M_F^*(X)$ with sample sizes of 100 and 1000 to estimate and infer the effects of the 2020 pandemic on the primary care and emergency room visits in the United States. The results indicate a significant decline in emergency room visits and a concomitant increase in primary care visits following the 2020 pandemic lock-downs. In recent years, interest in using linear multi-channel systems for distributed data collection, such as in sensor networks, has increased significantly. These systems, which consist of source sequences and multiple transmission channels with variable qualities, play a crucial role in applications that require rapid communication, such as emergency response and video streaming. The objective of designing linear multi-channel systems is to minimize the average transmission energy while meeting a set target bit error rate within a given number of attempts. The existing methods in literature often rely on a central controller or specific channel conditions, which can be impractical in real-world situations. In this paper, we propose a new approach to designing linear multi-channel systems that is adaptive, decentralized, and suitable for various channel scenarios. The proposed method, known as D2P2, utilizes historical channel data and the number of available channels to estimate the optimal transmission energy per bit. D2P2 operates in an online manner, adjusting its parameters for each transmission and can be applied to different channel conditions without any adjustments. The performance of D2P2 is evaluated through both theoretical analysis and multiple simulations, which show that it achieves comparable results to previously published adaptive methods while providing better performance when channel statistics are unknown. Additionally, D2P2 demonstrates superior performance compared to existing non-adaptive methods across various channel scenarios and source sequences. The proposed method also has the advantage of being more memory-efficient, which makes it more suitable for practical applications. Furthermore, D2P2 is shown to be applicable in managing distributed networks by utilizing a simple management protocol that allows nodes to join and leave the network freely. The results show that D2P2 can maintain optimal performance in dynamic network scenarios with both joining and leaving nodes. Overall, the proposed method has the potential to be a practical and efficient solution for a wide range of applications in linear multi-channel systems. This research evaluates various machine learning algorithms using a dataset on Notable Player (NP) log files from League of Legends. To address potential imbalances in the data, two balanced datasets were created, each with different feature probabilities for NPs and non-NPs. Training models on these balanced datasets helps mitigate the impact of dominance from the minority class. Ultimately, the best-performing models were identified and their features analyzed to determine which characteristics made players more likely to be classified as NPs. In the context of lung cancer and other diseases, the analysis of low-dose non-invasive Computed Tomography scans is significantly contributing to accurate diagnosis and treatment plans. Recently, with the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic, the use of CT scans has played a crucial role in diagnosing the virus by highlighting lung inflammation. Developing an automated system capable of accurately detecting COVID-19 from these scans could be vital in identifying infected patients rapidly, thus enhancing response times and reducing transmission rates. A time-distributed capsule network (TD-CP) architecture, designed for detecting patterns in sequential data, has been proposed for this application. By initially identifying lung regions, the model leverages capsule routing to ensure spatial and temporal information is correctly combined, resulting in a highly accurate fully-automated system. Evaluation on two separate datasets confirms the generalizability of the TD-CP, with detection accuracy exceeding human-level performance (87.1% vs. 86.5% on the Peking University dataset) and demonstrating exceptional adaptability when faced with data from multiple, diverse sources). Furthermore, the model's ability to scale with increased data was demonstrated by achieving 87.3% accuracy with an expanded dataset, highlighting its potential for continued improvement with larger, more diverse datasets in the future. A comparable level of performance was also achieved on the PaddleHub dataset (87.5% vs. 86.5% human-level performance), with the model outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods and demonstrating its potential for continued improvement with further training). Importantly, the proposed TD-CP detection system exhibits high sensitivity (83.9%) and specificity (90.4%), thus effectively balancing detection accuracy with minimal false positives. Consequently, the TD-CP offers significant potential as a diagnostic tool, capable of accurately detecting patterns in 3D image data. Its modular architecture also makes it easily applicable to a wide range of diagnostic tasks, with the ability to handle multi-channel data making it suitable for applications beyond COVID-19 detection. Future applications of this model could involve detecting patterns in imaging data for a range of diseases, such as lung cancer and other conditions requiring accurate diagnosis based on analysis of non-invasive Computed Tomography scans. Our study provides the first detailed analysis of AU Mic's atmosphere using far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectroscopy, observed over an 8-year period from FUV brightness minimum to intense flare activity. We analyzed the atmospheric structure and composition of AU Mic using CHIANTI 9.0.0, adjusting parameters for optimal fit and then comparing the minimum and flare-state spectra. The minimum spectrum matched a hot atmosphere with a temperature of 10^5 Kelvin and a metal enrichment 200 times greater than the solar value. This over-enrichment explains the high column density of heavy elements. However, the minimum spectrum did not require any heavy elements for the cooler layers (up to 10^4 Kelvin). In contrast, the flare spectra required additional cooler material (up to 10^3 Kelvin) and increased gas density (a factor of 20). We estimate the mass of AU Mic b and c to be 0.06 and 0.13 times the mass of the Earth, respectively. We observe no evidence of gas in the cooler layers within 10^3 kilometers of the exosphere. Instead, the gas is mostly confined to the hot FUV material, suggesting b and c could be in a scorching atmosphere extending far beyond their orbital distance. Our analysis also shows AU Mic's atmospheric structure is dynamic, with its upper atmosphere changing depending on whether the star is active or not. Further observations are needed to confirm these estimates and explore the dynamic atmosphere of AU Mic. An accelerating charged particle within a resistive medium experiences a drag caused by the medium's dynamic response to the particle's accelerating charge. This drag on accelerating charges is distinct from the Abraham-Lorentz process influenced by radiation recoil and is referred to as radiation reaction drag. The drag magnitude depends on factors including the particle's acceleration magnitude and direction, as well as the medium's properties. When the particle's acceleration is perpendicular to its velocity, the drag is symmetrical. Theoretical expressions for the drag are derived both analytically and through numerical integration, demonstrating consistent results. The derived drag expressions are comparable to those derived for a lossy medium under specific conditions. The total drag on the particle is shown to be the sum of the drag caused by the medium and the particle's mass due to acceleration in the medium. The derived equations can be used to model and analyze particle trajectories in systems with Coulomb and other short-range interactions within a resistive medium. The effect of the drag on these interactions is an acceleration-dependent downward curve. The same approach can be applied to longer-range interactions for comparison with experimental results, potentially revealing screening behavior. The derived equations may also be applied to other scenarios with acceleration-dependent forces. The derived total drag on the particle in a long-range interaction scenario can be used, for example, to model and analyze particle trajectories in systems with Coulomb interaction. Traditional methods for analyzing time-to-event data, such as the Kaplan-Meier method and Cox models, have been widely utilized, but they suffer from several limitations, including the inability to account for repeated events, multiple time scales, and complex covariates. To address these limitations, a novel framework known as the Multiple State Examination (mse) is introduced, which leverages multidimensional data analysis to handle multiple event types and scales through comprehensive life courses. mse is characterized by three key components: first-order partial autocorrelation analysis for detecting event risks and patterns, hierarchical regression for modeling concurrent and lagged effects, and clustering for characterizing individual life courses. mse's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to myocardial infarction data from the Stockholm Heart Study, showing that it offers valuable insights beyond what can be gained from examining individual event types in isolation. Efficient algorithms for simulations involving many molecules in solution require new approaches due to the inherent approximations involved in handling the solvent. One promising strategy is to divide the solvent into distinct regions where the same set of force fields can be applied, leading to potentially minimal impact on accuracy. This concept is built upon existing multi-scale methods, but extends to the molecular level, effectively becoming a multi-center integration technique. This paper describes such a scheme, implementing it into a dynamics simulation and comparing its results to simulations with more detailed water models. Additionally, we demonstrate the application of this method to electronic transport calculations through a quasi-equilibrium linear response approach. This approach allows us to validate our method by showing consistency with detailed models and demonstrating comparable accuracy with minimal computational overhead. This is achieved by demonstrating similar solvent configurations between detailed and simplified models, indicating that our multi-center integration technique can be an efficient solution for simulations in solution, specifically showing a $10^2$ fold speed-up with comparable accuracy. This work also opens up possibilities for future extensions to address specific solvent-specific interactions, effectively extending the scope of molecular dynamics simulations to address specific molecular and solvent-based transport phenomena in device applications. In formal verification, a widely accepted approach uses preconditions and postconditions to define functions.  This method provides a clear understanding of how functions operate, but it has its limitations, particularly with predicate-based postconditions that are challenging to express due to their restricted scope.  Higher-order logic, particularly in the HOL verification system, faces this limitation, making it difficult to define complex functions.  To address this issue, we propose an alternative method that incorporates timed definitions to describe functions over continuous time intervals.  By allowing postconditions to specify the temporal relationships between input and output, we can define functions more accurately and efficiently, even with postconditions that transcend predicate-based descriptions.  This approach enables more expressive definitions, facilitating meta-reasoning about these definitions.  In this study, we introduce timed definitions as a means of representing functions over time in HOL and demonstrate its potential by incorporating it into HOL as an extension, providing implementation examples, including the derivation of the square root function's fixed-point definition.  Our results confirm that timed definitions offer more expressive and efficient ways to describe functions, particularly those involving real numbers.  This work serves as a starting point for incorporating timed definitions as a standard feature in HOL and similar verification systems.  Additionally, we provide a supplementary online resource containing a collection of functions, both with preconditions and postconditions, as a practical example of using timed definitions in real-world applications.  This collection, available at https://github.com/steve-rtf/timed_definitions_hol, can be accessed and utilized by the verification community.  Finally, we plan to further develop this work by exploring its connections to other areas, including constructive analysis, dependent types, and state transition functions.  This research aims to ultimately expand the scope of functions definable in HOL to include those over more complex domains, such as the complex number system.  This goal is part of a broader objective to develop a comprehensive formalization of the real numbers as discussed in the report 'Real Numbers in HOL'.  This study is part of a larger project, available at https://github.com/steve-rtf/real_numbers_hol.  For related work and more detailed information, please refer to the supplementary material.  Furthermore, we intend to expand this work into a comprehensive formalization of the complex numbers, as initiated in the report 'Complex Numbers in HOL', available at https://github.com/steve-rtf/complex_numbers_hol. These states form separate energy islands within the otherwise continuous Weyl spectrum. The time-reversal-broken phase exhibits distinct features, including localized surface states and isolated energy pockets within the Weyl spectrum. As disorder levels increase, the time-reversal-broken phase shows a complex shift in momentum dependence. Our numerical results demonstrate that at intermediate disorder levels, the time-reversal-broken phase exhibits a combination of chevron and hexagonal patterns of momentum dependence. The transition between these two types of phase diagrams is triggered by a first-order phase transition. Conversely, at high disorder levels, the time-reversal-broken phase exhibits hexagonal momentum dependence for all flux densities. Our calculations also show that the time-reversal-broken phase persists across the entire Hofstadter model for any integer flux density. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the time-reversal-broken phase exhibits chiral symmetry breakdown as well. Additionally, at high disorder levels, the Weyl semi-metal exhibits isolated energy pockets within the Weyl spectrum, which form a ring structure. The width of this ring structure is influenced by the strength of the magnetic field and the disorder levels. Our findings provide a framework to understand phase transitions in topological materials, which can be experimentally verified through the analysis of symmetry and metal characteristics. The study of these materials may open new avenues for the investigation and understanding of topological phase transitions. This research paper explores the electronic properties of Mn-decorated silicene in relation to its environment. Using density functional theory, we studied the structural and electronic properties of Mn-decorated silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates of varying thickness. Our results indicate that Mn-decorated silicene is more stable when interacting with a single layer of boron nitride, as evidenced by the minimal out-of-plane displacement of the top layer of boron nitride atoms. Additionally, our findings show that the p orbitals of boron nitride have a marginal influence on the magnetism of adjacent Mn atoms, while hybridization between boron nitride and silicene leads to a loss of magnetism in adjacent Mn atoms. In contrast, Mn atoms at the edge of silicene or in the center remain magnetically stable. Overall, our research highlights the importance of exchange interactions and hybridization in determining the magnetism of Mn-decorated silicene. By combining machine learning and expert input, we're developing a system that can make informed decisions about a driver's competence under specific circumstances.
Our findings reveal that certain factors like weather and road quality have a substantial impact on driving behavior and should be taken into account by the assessment tool.
Moreover, our model shows that accounting for situational variables can significantly enhance the accuracy of the assessment.
By incorporating situational awareness into the assessment process, our study suggests that expert-driven adjustments to machine learning outputs can yield better results in real-world applications. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the ethical use of personal data and mitigate potential biases in driving performance evaluations. For modular forms of half-integers weight $k$, let $L(s,f)$ denote the associated L-functions. A specific value of $k$, namely $k=h$, is notable in that the L-functions yield distinct values at $s=\frac{1}{2}$ for non-equivalent forms. In terms of denominators of these values, specifically the L-function for $\Delta$ at $s=\frac{1}{2}$, Taniyama-Weil estimates suggest an upper bound of $10^{16}$, a finding initially attributed to K. Hashimoto. Using recent results on the representation of integers by class fields, we rederive this bound more straightforwardly and extend it to the denominators of the L-function values for non-holomorphic forms, including those of Maass forms. Moreover, under GRH, we find the denominators are no larger than $2^{40}\cdot e^{3}$. Notably, our method is independent of specific forms and applicable to any $\Delta$ and Maass form $f$ with weight greater than 0. In contrast, for forms of weight 0, specifically the L-function for $f$ on $\mathrm{GL}(2)$, the situation is more complex. However, for specific, well-studied cases, such as those of Hecke's fundamental forms, the denominators can be examined individually. For example, the denominator for $E_4(1)$ is found to be 5. Finally, while our method is versatile and applicable to a broad range of L-function values, the denominators may be quite large, a notable exception being the L-function values for forms with small weight, such as those of weight $-1$, which are computable. In these cases, the denominators can be determined precisely, as shown for the form $f(z)=\frac{E_7(z)}{E_{10}(z)}-1$. In this instance, the denominator at $s=\frac{1}{2}$ is found to be 319.9999999875, a value exceeding the bound provided by Taniyama-Weil estimates.}

These properties are known to be associated with specific numerical functions that relate the size of $S$ to the maximum independence number of $S$ within corresponding circumscribed graphs. Specifically, $S$ has a certain number of independent sets in circumscribed graphs when the size of $S$ does not surpass a particular upper limit that is determined by the maximum independence number of the circumscribed graphs. Furthermore, $S$ contains sets that form independent sets within circumscribed graphs when the size of $S$ meets a particular minimum requirement that is determined by the maximum independence number of the circumscribed graphs. These numerical functions are known to be associated with Hamiltonian cycles and pancyclicity in general graphs through the application of the distance matrix. Building upon these findings, we provide a detailed characterization of the numbers of independent sets in circumscribed graphs where the vertices of $S$ form specific types of cycles, such as $K_3$-free cycles, and we investigate the relationship between the numbers of independent sets in circumscribed graphs and the counts of independent vertices within $S$ within circumscribed graphs. To overcome this issue, we have introduced a new approach, where we combine sparse grid techniques with the residual based data fitting process to calculate the Koopman operator, resulting in significantly improved computational efficiency with no reduction in accuracy. Through numerical experiments on various complex systems, we have verified the high accuracy and computational efficiency of this new approach, achieving a maximum error reduction of five orders of magnitude, as well as substantial time savings with high-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this new method enables the solution of differential equations in a reduced dimension, resulting in a high degree of computational efficiency. This research introduces a novel method of solving the Schrödinger equation for an atom or molecule or ion in a strong direct current electric field. By modifying the potential energy to render the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues purely imaginary, we can simplify the mathematical representation. This modification has the effect of outsourcing complex boundary conditions, eliminating the need for separate treatment. We have developed an approach that combines numerical methods to solve for the Hamiltonian with a truncation of the many-body wave function. This approach enables us to directly calculate the energies of the system. Utilizing modern computational tools allows us to efficiently utilize a basis set consisting of both regular and outgoing wave functions, thereby accurately describing strong electric field continua. This method serves as a reliable tool for investigating atomic and molecular electronic structure within strong electric fields. Furthermore, we have determined the relevant outer scaling energy thresholds for various systems, which mark the point at which the electric field influences the system's electronic structure. These new energy limits provide crucial insights into the system's behavior and offer an alternative to existing approaches such as homotopy methods and perturbation theory. Additionally, we have demonstrated that the outer scaling method can be applied to various atomic and molecular systems, including H$^{+}$, H$_{2}^{+}$, He, Li$^{+}$, H$_{3}^{+}$, and the 2D electron gas. These results confirm that the outer scaling method accurately captures the system's behavior and its energy limits. A molecule with ferroelectric and caloric properties, ammonium sulfate ($\left[ NH _{4}\right] _{2 }^{2 }S O _{4}$}, has been studied to understand its extensive extensive entropy drop of 29.2 Ru/kmol when it ferroelectrically decomposes at 20.27 K. To accomplish this, researchers used quantum Monte Carlo methods to calculate the binding energy of the high-symmetry and lower-symmetry phases. Upon finding that the binding energy of the lower-symmetry phase is significantly lower than previously estimated, researchers clarified the long-standing assumption that the extensive entropy drop could be attributed to the level of entropy in the high-symmetry phase. In fact, the extensive entropy drop can be attributed to the level of phonon states present in the lower-symmetry phase, a phenomenon observed in the ferroelectric and structural phase transitions found in many materials. This discovery highlights the importance of considering extensive entropy in the context of thermodynamic cycles and offers an explanation for the unique caloric properties exhibited by ammonium sulfate. Moreover, researchers suggest that the extensive entropy drop could potentially be used to create thermomolecules with superior caloric capabilities. To support this idea, researchers used thermodynamic analysis to show that the extensive entropy drop can result in a substantial temperature-dependent caloric efficiency gain of up to 40% for a thermomolecule based on ammonium sulfate. To conclude, researchers propose the concept of extensive entropy as a key factor influencing the caloric capability of materials and ferroelectric phase transitions. Further exploration of this concept is expected to lead to the development of next-generation thermomolecules with enhanced caloric performance. In probabilistic learning, organisms calculate an optimal estimate of their chances of success, which serves as a foundation for making informed decisions. While most research has focused on the lower bound of this range (closest to 0), we investigated strategies that involve accepting a higher risk of failure in exchange for potential gains. Our study involved 22 healthy individuals making choices about receiving rewards or penalties in a series of games, which enabled us to assess their adaptive strategies. The results showed that individuals who employed suboptimal learning tactics tended to rely on these strategies consistently, whereas those who didn't, switched between different approaches. Additionally, brain activity in the midbrain was similar when using different techniques to measure performance, which could indicate that these regions distinguish between accurate and inaccurate predictions. Our findings suggest that there may be more to lower learning strategies than initially thought, and that further exploration of this range is necessary to fully understand the learning process. To tackle this issue, we introduce two novel algorithms. First, the CFS algorithm is specifically designed for unbounded time series and yields an O(nN^(1/delta)/epsilon^4) time complexity, surpassing current state-of-the-art efficiency by a factor of O(n/epsilon^4) compared to prior approaches. Building on this, the FRS algorithm is optimized for Gaussian time series and yields an O(n/epsilon^5) time complexity, representing an improvement of up to two orders of magnitude over existing solutions for such time series. Relative to the CFS algorithm, the FRS method leverages two key design enhancements: Firstly, it exploits the Gaussian time series properties to relax the Frechet distance constraint, thereby reducing the required number of computations. Secondly, it minimizes query processing time by identifying a bounded search area in the index for each repository time series. Both of these design improvements enable the FRS method to achieve a significant boost in efficiency, ultimately allowing it to handle more demanding workloads with higher query volumes. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms through comprehensive experiments and provide an in-depth analysis to identify avenues for future enhancements. This method is particularly useful for analyzing measurement distortions resulting from non-linear responses and background influences. While traditional unfolding techniques are effective for common quantum systems, they struggle with the increased complexity of advanced systems like superconducting qubits, which produce correlated error distributions. To overcome this limitation, we have adapted and expanded the iterative Bayesian unfolding technique to not only correct single-error measurements but also multiply-error measurements with high degrees of freedom. Our approach involves constructing a prior distribution based on system-specific knowledge and employing a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm to extract the underlying true distribution. We have tested our method using data from simulated quantum sensors with high-dimensional error distributions and found that it can achieve accurate results with minimal computational overhead. Moreover, our approach allows for the effective combination of measurements from multiple systems, thereby providing a framework for the scalable achievement of high-precision goals in quantum physics. As more humans interact with robots in various settings, interactions become crucial for effectively communicating intentions. In situations where humans and robots collaborate together, understanding each other's goals and plans enables smooth collaborations. However, when interactions are limited to non-colaborative contexts, robots primarily use visual and auditory cues to determine human actions. We argue that for safe and efficient human-robot interactions to occur, especially in environments where robots operate independently, clear and standardized communication of intentions is essential. We propose a framework that enables robots to follow standardized motion paths in response to human guidance, thereby conveying intentions. We introduce the concept of 'Shared Autonomy Scales' to measure the extent of autonomy in motion and investigate multiple communication channels, including gaze, touch, and verbal cues, to assess their effectiveness in prompting robotic motion along designated paths. We analyze various factors that could enhance or limit a robot's ability to follow motion directions based on human guidance. We demonstrate that by adjusting certain parameters, like touch-based guidance distance and verbal cue frequency, a robot can efficiently follow motion directions without straying from set paths. Our research demonstrates that human-robot interaction can be optimized for clear and standard communication of intentions, even in scenarios with limited interaction. The resulting framework has significant implications for developing independent robotic systems that safely interact with humans in various complex environments. We anticipate that our research will contribute positively to the advancement of robotic standards in areas such as human-robot collaboration, independent robotic systems, autonomous vehicles, and other applications requiring cooperative and independent interactions. As the robot moves through an area, diagrams at multiple scales are continuously updated in real-time, focusing on the immediate surroundings while also including redundant information for redundancy. To facilitate movement, a navigation technique is presented that enables the robot to make decisions based on a diagram representation. A simulator designed to mimic the appearance of sonar data has been used to test the robot's ability to learn and navigate using this representation. Results show that a robot employing this method successfully navigates through unknown environments with minimal loss, even when sonar data quality is compromised due to sensor noise or missing readings. Moreover, our method outperforms competing navigation techniques that rely on random exploration. To provide further insights into the representation's capabilities, we have also created an extended version of this research, where a robot using diagram information explores and maps an unfamiliar environment. To the best knowledge of our knowledge base, this research marks the first instance where a representation of this type has been successfully applied to navigation and mapping in unknown environments. A comprehensive evaluation of this extension is presented, comparing its capabilities to existing mapping algorithms, revealing that our representation yields more accurate maps with better coverage, as demonstrated through a detailed analysis. We have observed that a robot employing this extension recovers approximately 75% of an environment's area, significantly outperforming other top methods like IQL and Kernel-Based Mapping, which recover only 58% and 43%, respectively. We have also observed that while our method takes the longest to map an environment among the compared algorithms, its maps exhibit the lowest level of distortion, as a result of its focus on maintaining topological consistency and detail. This paper presents a groundbreaking variational method for simultaneously reconstructing and analyzing CT data collected from complex, multi-energy detectors with diverse sensor configurations. By formulating a non-convex energy functional that accounts for image smoothness, image physics-based constraints, sensor noise correction, and optimized weight adaptation, we address the challenge of adapting X-ray attenuation coefficients to accommodate various sensor types during CT data acquisition. Due to the presence of several non-convex components, we develop an efficient majorized semi-smooth algorithm to solve this issue. By testing our method with simulated and actual data from a laboratory setup with a single-source X-ray system equipped with different detectors, we successfully remove visible noise impressions, recover the physical X-ray flux, and accurately separate and identify various materials present in the scene. The results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over traditional methods that address these challenges individually. This research examines the impact of electron spillover and nonlocal behavior on gap plasmons in ultra-small metallic inclusions. These tiny structures, known as nano islands, are embedded in a gap that becomes progressively thinner, approaching zero. To analyze this scenario, we employ two distinct electron gas models: a local approach based on Thomas-Fermi and a nonlocal quantum model grounded in Dirac's equation. By integrating these electron state descriptions with the Random Phase Approximation, we derive linearized responses and compare the electronic properties, electron densities, and potential distributions generated by the two models. As the gap dimension becomes extremely small, our analysis reveals a nonobvious convergence of the two models, leading us to conclude that a quantum description is essential for understanding nano island physics. Our research further demonstrates that nonlocal electron behavior yields more substantial low-frequency enhancements of electron spillover compared to the local approach, underscoring the critical role of nonlocality in ultra-small metallic inclusions. Additionally, we demonstrate that nonlocal electron behavior generates an induced positive charge in the nano island when surrounded by a thin electron layer, emphasizing the importance of this phenomenon in ultra-small metallic inclusions. Our research also explores the impact of nonlocal electron behavior on nano island resonance modes and reveals that these modes are highly influenced by both nonlocal and local electron behavior. By comparing the nonlocal and local responses to electromagnetic excitations, we demonstrate that these modes exhibit distinct low-frequency enhancements. Our research further shows that these modes are highly sensitive to nonlocal electron behavior, with nonlocality inducing a more substantial low-frequency enhancement compared to the local case. Overall, our research highlights the critical importance of nonlocal electron behavior in ultra-small metallic inclusions and nano island physics. Contextual named entity retrieval (CNER) is a critical component of entity-centric applications such as question answering, with current methods falling short in responding to complex queries with numerous entities and their interconnected contexts. For instance, a question like "Who are the running backs for the Dallas Cowboys?" demands not only relevant entities (running backs and Dallas Cowboys) but also context-specific responses related to other entities like (games, sports, etc.) implied by the query. The existing CNER datasets and evaluation methods are inadequate in addressing this challenge. To fill this gap, we introduce a new evaluation metric and a dataset to assess CNER performance in responding to contextually dependent queries with multiple entities. Unlike traditional evaluation methods, our approach focuses on term-by-term relevance and requires retrieved responses to contain target entities along with relevant context terms. Our new dataset, called CoNer, is designed to overcome the limitations of existing CNER datasets by featuring complex queries, diverse contexts, and a need for good responses to contain more than just target entities. Our analysis highlights significant CNER shortcomings, and we introduce several strategies to demonstrate how enhancing CNER capabilities can lead to better responses to complex queries with multiple entities. Furthermore, our study explores the potential of pre-trained transformer models as a viable solution for CNER. The proposed evaluation method and the CoNer dataset can be utilized for CNER evaluation, and the data can be accessed through an accompanying GitHub repository at https://github.com/aiharsha/CoNer. The CNER results are presented in a CER system which can be accessed through the link at https://github.com/aiharsha/CER-system. The results of our study reveal a considerable gap in CNER capabilities, and we believe the proposed method and the CoNer dataset can facilitate further advancements in this area. Time-based data analysis is gaining prominence, yet methods for visually analyzing and engaging with time-series and longitudinal data remain underdeveloped. Human beings are more adept at comprehension and memory recall when engaging with time-based data through narrative methods. Drawing inspiration from the power of storytelling, this paper introduces 'ChronoPlots,' a novel visual representation that shows changes over time in multiple categories, and 'LongitudinalPlots,' which tracking progress in multiple categories over a period of time. Both novel forms are interactive and can be explored in 3 dimensions. By combining narratives, we can highlight changes, trends and patterns in the data, illustrating stories behind time-based and longitudinal data. ChronoPlots and LongitudinalPlots were put to the test with real-life data sets – a COVID-19 vaccine study and a bike-sharing pattern study – and the results demonstrate that engaging with time-based and longitudinal data through narrative methods fosters a deeper sense of connection and understanding, enhancing audience participation. This research opens doors for further development and implementation of interactive, engaging time-based data analysis methods, encouraging a deeper understanding and more effective communication of data. The study's code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/kevinschuirel/chronoplots. The associated prototype is available at https://chronoplots.herokuapp.com/.

Personalized medicine seeks to meet the unique health needs of diverse populations by leveraging various data sources. However, incorporating multiple types of data poses significant challenges to medicine due to its inherent heterogeneity. To address these challenges, graph neural networks have been explored for use in personalized healthcare. This study presents an heterogeneous resemblance graph neural network (HH-GNN) designed for electronic health record (EHR) analysis, where nodes represent healthcare recipients and edges signify similarities based on their EHR data. The proposed HH-GNN approach relies on local and global similarity representations to aggregate and combine node information, thus capturing both local details and global heterogeneity. Experimental evaluations using real-world EHR datasets demonstrate that HH-GNN achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, showcasing its effectiveness for EHR analysis. Additionally, the integrated system enables healthcare professionals to identify and establish connections between patients based on their medical records and provide tailored recommendations. This research has the potential to promote the incorporation of heterogeneous data for better healthcare outcomes. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/whu9110/hgnn. The EHR dataset used in this study can be accessed through https://figshare.com/datver. Further details on this work can be found at https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4896/17/15/744. At the interface between the soft surface and the electrolyte, a region of variable charge is introduced, allowing for charge variation with distance. Utilizing a mean-field approach, the effects of solvent polarization and electrostatic interactions on the structural arrangement of ions are considered. An integral equation is solved to obtain density profiles of ions and the solvent, while the charge distribution at the interface is determined through a Lagrange multiplier method. As a result, the density profiles of ions and the solvent, electrostatic potential, and the surface charge density can be obtained as functions of solution parameters, including temperature, electrolyte concentration, and the dielectric properties of the solvent. Furthermore, the influence of solvent polarization on the structural arrangement of ions and the electrostatic potential is found to be significant when the electrolyte concentration is low and the dielectric properties of the solvent are close to that of water. The model is applied to a system resembling a biological membrane with a variable charge profile, and the results are compared with molecular dynamics simulations to validate the model and identify regions requiring further consideration. Automated software extraction techniques from natural language documents are highly needed as manual transcription and analysis consume considerable time, hindering progress in various areas such as software genealogy research. Existing studies employ structured documents or incorporate domain-specific features and quality control measures. In contrast, this research tackles the more complex challenge of analyzing unstructured text, like academic papers and source code repositories, which provide essential historical context. Our study develops a multi-step pipeline integrating advanced language models to replicate software extraction techniques for a sample of 150 studies, demonstrating the reliability and accuracy of our methods. The proposed pipeline is now publicly accessible and aims to facilitate software extraction, promoting increased research productivity. Our data and toolsets are available at https://doi.org/10.6100/ETHZ-RA-2022-7 and https://github.com/epfl-asi/software-extraction. The pipeline was validated using 150 recent research papers as well as two books on cloning and product line engineering, yielding promising results and highlighting the importance of vocabulary knowledge for accurate software extraction. Our study also identifies potential areas for improvement, such as fine-tuning the incorporation of semantic knowledge for enhanced feature recognition. Furthermore, as software extraction yields numerous annotated samples, which can be utilized for training and testing the performance of language models in software-related naming and description tasks. Our study contributes to the development of software extraction techniques, which can be applied to a broader range of unstructured text types, and bridges the gap between software engineering and NLP by applying cutting-edge language models to software engineering problems. The study also sheds light on the evolution of software engineering naming conventions over time. In line with our research goals, we release the extracted software entities for 150 recent research papers on software engineering, totaling over 1,000 unique software entities, which can be leveraged for data augmentation, sentiment analysis, or scientific impact assessment in the future. In addition, we plan to extend our study to encompass a broader range of software engineering domains and research applications. However, as the proposed method relies on large and high-quality training datasets, which are typically scarce in the software engineering field, we recognize the need for more advanced language models that integrate semantic knowledge to further enhance software extraction accuracy. In particular, our study indicates that word embeddings can be improved by incorporating domain-specific knowledge, which is essential for accurate software extraction. In summary, our research aims to bridge the gap between software engineering and NLP, and contributes to the development of software extraction techniques that can be applied to a broader range of unstructured text types.

This study investigates energy-saving potential in wireless networks with high traffic by examining the combined effects of network coding and time division multiple access (TDMA). Following an initial analysis of a network with multiple sources, multiple relays, and a single destination, we introduce a novel scheduling and power allocation strategy that maximizes throughput while minimizing overall network energy consumption. Our proposed strategy, called collaborative network coding, involves simultaneous data transmission and network coding, which reduces energy consumption and increases throughput. To optimize this strategy, we formulated a bi-objective optimization problem and solved it using the Pareto optimal method, using a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to obtain the best solutions. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the existence and characteristics of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov states in response to localized non-equivalent spin impurities situated near the surface of a superconducting material. This theoretical framework, grounded in relativistic Dirac formalism, offers a versatile and rigorous approach for predicting various impurity arrangements on superconducting surfaces. This model theory was applied to investigate Mn impurities on the surface of niobium in order to prepare for experimental examination of related phenomena using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Results revealed the presence of distinct YSR states associated with individual Mn impurities as well as multiple YSR states within clusters consisting of two and three Mn atoms. Furthermore, through simulation and theoretical prediction, the relationships between low-energy split peaks and inter-impurity distances were established for various cluster configurations. These predictions are anticipated to facilitate accurate comparison with experimental findings using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Ultimately, the established theory and results demonstrate satisfactory agreement with experimental observations. This successful application of the developed theory to systems under investigation effectively validates the theoretical framework and provides valuable insights for interpreting experimental results, specifically those involving scanning tunneling spectroscopy. Additionally, the theoretical framework, grounded in relativistic formalism, offers a versatile and efficient approach for predicting and analyzing a wide array of impurity arrangements on superconducting surfaces. This methodology may be adapted and applied to investigate various systems, including those consisting of multiple impurities and nanoclusters on superconducting surfaces. Future research directions and relevant questions for consideration are also discussed.
