We've developed a new framework that identifies mistakes in dynamical systems models by using a machine learning algorithm to analyze short, observed system trajectories. Even with limited data available, this framework can learn about the system's behavior and detect if the model is incorrect. This is because, in many cases, there are short, observable differences between a system's actual behavior and its corresponding model. These differences can be learned using time series data from various points within the system, without needing additional information about how the system interacts or detailed analyses. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness by applying it to simple examples, including linear systems and the Lorenz equations. In each case, the learned model represents the system's behavior over different time spans and identifies any discrepancies. This learned correction can then either correct the original model or be used as a model in its own right. This research presents a new approach to using machine learning for qualitative model learning and detection, opening up possibilities for its use in various settings where short, observed data is available. This could be in scientific domains, such as studying short, highly chaotic systems, or in other areas, such as monitoring systems in real-time for model failures. Several potential applications and further research directions are discussed at the end of this study. This work and its associated code can be found at the provided repository link. This work was supported by the methods and resources described in our related study, published at IJCAI 2021. Specifically, this includes details on our initial attempt to use machine learning for model mistake detection in dynamical systems. Although the current study presents a new approach, we found that some of the underlying concepts proved useful and are leveraged here. High-resolution polarized light maps also show that the core's southern tip has a highly organized magnetic field structure, indicating that magnetic forces can contain the core's collapse. This paper investigates a set addition problem where multiple options can be added to a given set, and users can express preferences over the resulting sets by ranking them. A unique challenge in this task is determining when to stop adding items to the set, and a novel contextual preference learning approach is proposed to address this issue. Unlike non-contextual methods that learn item preferences in isolation, the proposed method models user decisions as an incremental process with a single attribute: the current set composition. A comparative evaluation of contextual and non-contextual models demonstrates the former's superiority in tackling the set addition problem. Notably, the contextual model's performance improves significantly when its capacity for sequential reasoning is enhanced. Additionally, experimental results show that incorporating a capability for batch processing, as seen in the expert model, and incorporating diverse contextual attributes can further boost the model's effectiveness. A thorough analysis of the models' learned representations and decision-making strategies through SHAP values and concept anchoring experiments is also presented. Overall, the research highlights the set addition problem as an effective benchmark for evaluating contextual preference learning methods and their applications in practical settings. The research code can be found at https://github.com/ashish97/contextual-set-addition on GitHub. Our goal is to examine the connections between thermodynamics and dynamics in polymers that lead to glass formation. We focus on the role of configurational entropy and temperature-dependent relaxation times, using statistical mechanics to develop expressions based on molecular structure that can be tested experimentally. Next, we investigate how dynamics affect thermodynamic properties, particularly the entropy and free energy, in systems stuck in local minima due to slow dynamics. We then explore non-equilibrium, quasi-static cooling protocols to assess the damage inflicted by rapid temperature changes and introduce a new cooling rate parameter to measure this impact. These relationships apply broadly to simple and complex polymer fluids, as long as they consist of flexible molecules. We also provide a link to existing theories while identifying areas for improvement and offering suggestions for further research. We support our work with detailed simulations of polymer fluids that confirm our theoretical findings. We demonstrate that measuring configurational entropy dynamically (from relaxation times) or thermodynamically (from partition functions and combinatorics) yield nearly identical results. We show that slow dynamics at low temperatures correspond to high cooling rates, resulting in destructive excitations and substantial damage. We validate our approach by comparing it to cooling protocols and examine the cooling rate's influence on the onset of crystallization and the formation of amorphous structures. We find that increasing molecular structure complexity, polymer branchiness, and chain length, as well as decreasing density, delay crystallization and damage formation. Finally, we provide a simple expression to calculate dynamic viscosity from relaxation times and configurational entropy. We hope this work will contribute to a new understanding of polymer dynamics and glass formation. We have made our code available, enabling researchers to simulate polymer fluids of varying complexity using the open-source package LAMMPS. Additionally, we provide a related publication that explores cooling rate effects in aging and stress relaxation. Further details can be found in our doctoral thesis, particularly Chapter 5 and Chapter 6. A significant concern in large language models' (LLMs) behavior arises from their potential to reject or distort user inputs, resulting in the propagation of misinformation. To advance understanding and mitigation strategies for these behaviors, this study investigates the development of rejection behaviors in language models, including their likelihood, content, and responses to repeated queries. We found that, similar to humans, large language models initially accept new information and only reject it when it significantly diverges from their existing knowledge. Moreover, models tend to provide repetitive responses to the same questions, indicating inflexibility in their reasoning. Our results provide essential insights for developing and improving rejection-handling capabilities in LLMs for real-world applications. They will be made available on a new benchmark called REJ, evaluating an LLM's ability to process rejection adequately. This benchmark aims to facilitate further research into rejection behaviors and inform developers and users about the limitations of current LLMs. We hope the benchmark will contribute to the development of more robust, rejection-savvy models in the future. Despite the expectation that the critical point should correspond to an interacting conformal fixed point, we surprisingly find that the fixed point is instead non-interacting, with a conformal spectrum consistent with that of a free theory, at all values of the coupling strength. However, we observe that while thermal properties are sufficient to determine the behavior of the theory, entanglement entropy falls short of this criterion. The existence of diffuse gamma-ray emission in galaxy clusters is well-documented, 
originating from various particle-proton interactions within the intracluster medium. 
Despite these localized particle acceleration sites being dispersed throughout 
the clusters, the corresponding diffuse gamma-ray emission is observed to be 
uniformly distributed across the sky, thanks to the clusters' symmetrical 
morphology. It has been hypothesized that the gamma-ray emission resulting from 
particle interactions in the dispersion medium, accounting for the uniform 
distribution, is consistent with the clusters' diffuse emission being dominated 
by particle-proton interactions. However, we now present findings indicating that 
the gamma-ray emission resulting from particle interactions in the dispersion 
medium is actually insufficient to explain the clusters' diffuse emission, 
leading to the conclusion that the primary source of the diffuse gamma-rays is 
still unidentified. Furthermore, we show that the gamma-ray emission resulting 
from relativistic electrons in clusters is also unable to account for the 
observed diffuse emission, leaving the origin of the gamma-ray emission still 
unresolved. Possible explanations for the unidentifed source of the diffuse 
gamma-rays are explored. The findings presented contribute to an enhanced 
understanding of the complex astrophysical processes governing galaxy 
clusters, potentially providing valuable insights for the identification of the 
unresolved source of diffuse gamma-rays. The research further highlights the 
importance of the discrete sources of gamma-ray emission originating from 
galaxy clusters in shaping the observed diffuse emission. The investigation 
utilized data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope and included 48 galaxy 
clusters, providing a rich dataset for understanding the astrophysical 
processes governing galaxy clusters and the cosmos. The research aims to 
ultimately facilitate the identification of the unresolved source of the 
diffuse gamma-rays through a deeper understanding of the astrophysical 
processes at play. The research has been peer-reviewed and published in the

This study examines the potential implications of primordial features within the primordial primordial black hole density spectrum on the cosmic microwave background radiation data, focusing on the CMB anisotropies resulting from the decay of primordial black holes. To accurately assess the effects of primordial features, we develop a classical cosmological collider physics framework, which enables computation of tree-level soft processes for arbitrary background geometries. Our framework applies to systems with spin, accounting for the redshift of soft modes and confirming prior research results in the case of a flat universe. Additionally, our work extends the state-of-the-art by: 1) incorporating non-flat geometries, 2) supporting featureless spectra calculations for benchmarking purposes, 3) expanding calculations to include dipolar modulation, and 4) evaluating the sensitivity of CMB data to primordial features for both Planck and future Simons Observatory data sets. Our results demonstrate that with the latter data set, features corresponding to $k \gtrreeq 10^{-4}$ can be detected at the $2\sigma$ level, while those with lower $k$ values may be detectable if the feature amplitude reaches $10^{-3}$. However, detection proves impossible with the former data set. We investigate the divergence properties of two categories of groups: the generalised Thompson groups and the braided-Thompson groups, using a technique that combines topological and metric analysis. In the case of the generalised Thompson groups, our main result establishes a metric analysis under the Hausdorff metric, thereby characterising diversity for word maps. Additionally, we prove that diversity is conserved across subgroup maps when the underlying subgroups share specific characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the diversity of composite maps is determined by the diversity of individual maps involved. These conserved and composite properties of diversity align with analogous findings in the braided-Thompson groups, as determined by an alternate metric analysis. In the braided case, our results are refined by introducing a diversity invariant similar to the Thompson's group V example and showing its relation to a braided version of the VAFS property. We also explore the implications of our findings for the generation of subgroups within the braided groups. Ultimately, our research aims to lay the groundwork for a large-scale metric analysis of the braided Thompson groups, which may lead to further applications in the study of foliations and flow dynamics. A fundamental concept in the Stone-Stewart theory involves a specific class of orthogonal polynomials defined in relation to a logarithmic weight on a specific interval. The logarithmic weight's singular nature presents a unique challenge, making it necessary to first establish the unique polynomial $Q_j$ for each $j$, which in turn enables the creation of a sequence of polynomials orthogonal to the weight and subsequently computes their coefficients. The final step leads to the determination of the asymptotic behavior of these orthogonal polynomials as they approach the boundary of their interval of definition, a calculation complicated by the weight's logarithmic influence. The calculated asymptotics include precise information about the limits of the polynomials and their derivatives at the boundary points, as well as the form of the weight function in this context. The analysis provided in this work is accompanied by specific examples of weights that may or may not satisfy the required conditions for asymptotic calculations. A notable example, involving an attempt to apply the standard theory to a weight function whose square is logarithmically periodic but the function itself is not, highlights the necessity of a modified approach. Another example, derived from a Stieltjes transformation of the Jacobi polynomial's weight $x^{2\alpha-1}(1-x^2)^{\beta+1}$, demonstrates the theory's applicability in this context. Finally, a weight function proposed by one of the co-authors in an earlier work, which was found not to be positive on the interval $[0,1)$ due to a mistake in its construction, serves as another example for analysis. The theory is applied in this case to recover the positive counterpart of this weight, which in turn allows for a sequence of monic polynomials $P_{2\alpha-1}(x|\p,0)$, orthogonal to $\p(x)(1-x)^{\beta+1}$ on $[0,1)$, to be computed and analyzed asymptotically as they approach the right boundary of their interval of definition. The calculated limits and forms for these polynomials and their associated recurrence coefficients enable predictions about their behavior as they approach the boundary of their interval of definition. Crowdsourcing has proven effective for gathering data, but it is hindered by low retention rates and variability among workers.  Understanding which tasks attract skilled and qualified workers is crucial for effective crowdsourcing.  Previous studies indicate that skilled workers prefer tasks with clear instructions, relevant feedback, and competitive pay - however, they do not provide a comprehensive analysis of how task characteristics impact worker participation and performance.  Our study examines the task characteristics that influence participation and quality by analyzing MTurk tasks through three theoretical perspectives - signaling theory, task design theory, and social psychology theory.  Analyzing 136 tasks created by 80 different researchers, we identified key characteristics that impact worker behavior, such as pay, quality requirements, and consistency of instructions.  These findings can inform the design of Crowdsourcing initiatives, ultimately improving the outcome.  Additionally, we provide best practices and recommendations based on our analysis, suggesting that while pay is crucial, it is not the sole determining factor of worker participation.  Our research also demonstrates that factors such as feedback and quality expectations can improve participation rates.  Ultimately, our study aims to improve the design of Crowdsourcing initiatives to produce high-quality results.  The analysis and insights from our study can be applied to various fields within the information systems discipline.  Our findings suggest that future research methods should prioritize understanding the underlying psychological and social factors that impact worker behavior, such as perceived risk, autonomy, and motivation.  Additionally, our study highlights the importance of evaluating task characteristics through multi-faceted lenses of theory, enabling effective comparisons between tasks and designs.  The outcome of our analysis indicates that future research methods should prioritize understanding the underlying psychological and social factors that impact worker behavior, such as perceived risk, autonomy, and motivation. Text-image matching is an important component of various computer vision tasks, including image retrieval and object recognition. Current techniques primarily employ pre-trained models and focus on image features. In contrast, text features are often directly extracted from input text and do not consider the structure and semantics of sentences. This paper presents a novel text-image matching network called TS2-Net, incorporating a shifting and selecting token transformer module. It simultaneously captures contextual and selective text features by shifting and selecting specific tokens based on contextual cues. When pre-trained models are not accessible, TS2-Net can be used without fine-tuning to achieve competitive performance on Text-Clip Retrieval (TCR) tasks. Additionally, incorporating it into popular transformer models can enhance their performance by 4% and 2% respectively on MSRVTT-1M and MSRVTT datasets. Key strengths of TCR include its lightweight nature, efficiency, and generalizability, making it an ideal tool for analysis and understanding of text-image matching. Furthermore, TS2-Net can also be applied to other text-based visual tasks where token shifting and selection are allowed. It is well documented that taste-changing neutral currents were a major concern in the early days of the Tevatron, with many contributing factors remaining unclear at that time. In this research, we explore taste-changing neutral currents in top quark pair production, which can serve as a key indicator of new physics beyond the Standard Model. Our analysis reveals two categories of taste-changing neutral currents: those involving right-handed gamma-5 dileptons and top quarks, and those involving cohomological contributions in one-loop diagrams. These new channels have several advantages, including enhanced sensitivity to new physics at high energy levels and a more defined connection with neutral currents observed in neutrino experiments. Furthermore, we propose a new set of observables that can help mitigate jet-related uncertainties and significantly boost the potential for discovering new physics in top quark pair events. Our study demonstrates that taste-changing neutral currents in top quark pair production are a powerful tool for exploring beyond-SM physics. Finally, we show that various new models, including triplet Higgsinos and LEP-stable heavy neutral leptons, can manifest as resonances or new physics within this channel, thus underscoring its potential for further investigation. Overall, our analysis suggests that taste-changing neutral currents in top quark pair production are a valuable area of further investigation in experimental particle physics. Our findings are presented in detail, along with associated tables and figures. Moreover, in response to recent research indicating potential CP-violation in top quark decays, which could be linked to taste-changing neutral currents, we expand our analysis to examine these effects in detail, revealing that while these processes are currently very small, they may be a significant indicator of new physics if observed at a significance of more than three standard deviations. Our analysis is presented in figure six. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential for taste-changing neutral currents in top quark pair production to be a major area of investigation in particle physics, particularly through the study of top quark decays at future high-energy colliders. aimed at reducing background: (i) using a muon stopper to terminate beams at the
detector entrance, (ii) implementing a fast beam abort to swiftly remove

We introduce a data condensation approach called Spartan, allowing large datasets to be compressed into a minimal set of representative key points using a differentiable method. Unlike existing methods, Spartan does not rely on clustering or projection techniques. Instead, it leverages the idea of optimal transportation with a condensed target distribution having near-zero values. By introducing a set of implicit sparsity variables, Spartan transforms this problem into one where these variables can be optimized efficiently using stochastic gradient descent. We prove the existence and uniqueness of the optimal target distribution for self-organization, and we demonstrate Spartan on various datasets, achieving significant speedup over current methods. Furthermore, Spartan enables the integration of compressive datasets into deep neural network models, allowing for efficient training and validation in environments with limited memory resources. We showcase Spartan's effectiveness in compressing activation maps for visual tasks and in reducing the size of hand-written digits for efficient classification. Additionally, we showcase applications in generative models, latent representations, and unsupervised learning tasks, including reinforcement learning in the game of Tetris. Our results show that Spartan achieves state-of-the-art results on MNIST, Tetris, and other tasks, while outperforming other methods with superior quality, runtime, and memory usage. The method is available at https://github.com/alexandershefelin/spartan.

Art historians seek to noninvasively date mysterious brushprints discovered at random, which are thought to originate from unknown artists from a specified time period. By assuming that brushmarks from the same artist exhibit temporal continuity, we develop a statistical model that unites both artistic data and historical timing constraints. To optimize this union, we implement an integrated differential brush process and draw upon the computationally efficient structure of Gaussian covariance functions. To efficiently estimate unknown parameters, we reduce the computationally complex nondifferentiable problem into a series of simpler, convex subsurface problems. To address issues of nonidentifiability and nonconvexity, we develop novel subsurface-based methods for inferring artist relationships and group clustering. To extend our model to high-dimensional data, we develop a representation learning approach, utilizing a variational autoencoder, to generate representative embeddings for both artistic brushmarks and timing constraints, thus enabling joint inference of both artists and timing via a single subsurface-based method. Our proposed methods demonstrate strong empirical performance across various artistic periods, including British watercolor painters and 19th-century French impressionists. Notably, our model has been successfully applied to a recently discovered impressionist brushmark, allowing art historians to infer both the brushmark's artist and timing, and further shedding light on the mysterious world of artistic history. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package brushest. Future research will involve the development of adjacent models, including a brushmark detection model based on differential operators. The proposed methods can be directly extended to other types of continuous data such as electronic health records. The proposed approach is part of an ongoing collaboration with the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the National Gallery to apply the methods to their respective collections. Each of these added features is implemented through the use of multiple photon diagrams achieved with the help of the CKYMC Monte Carlo parton shower generator. Comprehensive comparisons between KKMCee's predictions and established, high-precision codes demonstrate the reliability of the newly created events, which are subsequently made available in the form of a public interface with the FastJet package for fast simulation use cases. In England, local tracing partnerships were established to expand the reach of contact tracing and fill gaps left by the national program, particularly in areas experiencing high COVID-19 case rates.  Contact tracing is the process of identifying and informing individuals infected with a disease to their recent contacts, asking them to self-isolate for a set period.  A study assessed the performance of these partnerships and the national program using COVID-19 case data from 28 English cities where the partnerships were active.  The research found that, on average, the partnerships identified 25% to 38% more contacts per case than the national program.  A simulation revealed that, in cities with high case rates, the partnerships reduced hospitalizations by 5% to 8%.  Analysis suggested that, in cities where the partnerships were active early on, they had a more significant impact on case rate reductions than the national program alone would have had.  A quantitative assessment of the partnerships' efficiency using metrics such as contacts per case, case finding, and isolation rates did not yield conclusive results, suggesting that the impact of the partnerships varied depending on the city and time of establishment.  A major factor believed to have contributed to these disparities was the variation in the amount of resources allocated to the partnerships by the government. A key ontology characteristic is its ability to organize vast amounts of information, comprising subject class hierarchies and descriptive properties. However, current visualization tools primarily focus on illustrating hierarchical structures, while overlooking other essential aspects. To address this limitation, we propose OntoPlot, a innovative visual representation of ontologies that effectively communicates non-hierarchical associations between subject classes. OntoPlot's design combines an overview page for subject classes and a detailed exploration page featuring associated concepts, allowing users to analyze concepts linked to individual classes or compare relationships across multiple subjects. To enhance user interaction, we incorporate a innovative zooming mechanism, supported by intuitive controls for customizing the display of subject classes and concept importance. To assess OntoPlot's usability and effectiveness, we conducted a comparative study involving 32 participants using Plalistia, a large ontology containing detailed information about aquatic life, against ClassBrowser, a commercially available browser. As such, the system has a wide range of practical applications, including supporting research in aquatic science for students working on the Plalistia project. By evaluating faux throws with point-of-release errors both above and below the specified point, we found that participants tend to prefer the throw that appears to have the correct technique, even if the actual trajectory differs. Researchers led by S. C. A. Russell studied how solutions of the complex DaRy-Stewartson II equations evolve over time. They found that in one aspect of this problem, the behavior of solutions is closely linked to the properties of solutions of the DaRy-Stewartson I equations. They examined this aspect using the reflection coefficient of solutions at different points in space and space-time. Based on analytical calculations and computer simulations, they found that the reflection coefficient can exhibit two distinct behaviors, one that is stable and highly predictable and another that is less stable and more prone to surprises. Furthermore, they discovered that the less stable behavior is linked to solutions that contain certain types of modulated waves. Finally, they found that when this less stable behavior occurs, the reflection coefficient can lead to a loss of precision over time, a phenomenon that is not present in the stable case. To confirm these findings, they compared them to results from computer simulations and found a good match. 

In particular, when examining the less stable case, they found that the reflection coefficient can exhibit significant variations, growing or decreasing rapidly over short periods of time. They observed this behavior in computer simulations where the intensity of modulated waves reached a critical threshold, causing the system to transition into a less stable state. 

Conversely, when examining the stable case, they found that the reflection coefficient can exhibit predictable and highly stable behavior, changing gradually over long periods of time. 

In summary, they found that the stable case is characterized by a stable and highly predictable behavior where the reflection coefficient changes gradually over long periods of time. In contrast, the less stable case is characterized by a less stable and more prone to surprises behavior where the reflection coefficient can exhibit significant variations, growing or decreasing rapidly over short periods of time. 

This research provides new insights into how solutions of the complex DaRy-Stewartson II equations can evolve over time, shedding light on the properties of these solutions and their behavior. 

The discovery of two distinct cases, one stable and one less stable, is a significant breakthrough in understanding these solutions and their behavior. 

By linking the less stable case to the properties of modulated waves, they were able to gain a deeper understanding of these waves and their role in the less stable case. 

By comparing their analytical results to computer simulations, they were able to confirm their findings and provide a link between theoretical and computational results.

Developing efficient NLP models that are both compact and cost-effective is becoming increasingly important despite the challenges involved, especially in languages with limited data and resources. Two such techniques used to address these challenges are quantization and distillation. This paper compares the stability and effectiveness of these approaches in reducing the size of low-resource machine translation models, focusing particularly on how they impact translation accuracy and model stability. Our findings reveal that while they can significantly reduce model size, they are vulnerable to instability, particularly when dealing with more extreme compression methods. Crucially, however, it appears that distillation is more consistent in its performance, even when pushed to more extreme levels, suggesting that distillation may offer a more reliable route to creating compact, low-resource MT models. To further improve the efficiency of these models, our research proposes a novel method of combining distillation, involving the training of multiple, smaller models on a larger, more compact model for improved performance. Our results demonstrate that this approach can lead to significant gains in performance, especially when compared to individual models trained in isolation. Ultimately, this research offers valuable insights and approaches for developing efficient, low-resource MT models, while highlighting areas for further improvement in the future. The effectiveness of image augmentation in reducing the labelled data requirement for computer vision tasks has been well-documented. This research investigates the application of image augmentation for the specific biomedical task of pneumonia segmentation. Our findings suggest that a combination of augmentation techniques, particularly those involving colour constancy, discrete rotation, and mirror reflection, can significantly improve model performance and reduce the need for labelled data by up to 75% in terms of accuracy and dice coefficient for the specific biomedical segmentation task of pneumonia detection. This outcome implies that image augmentation can be an efficient data augmentation strategy to obtain comparable results with labelled data when such resources are limited. Current models excel at producing descriptive text, yet controlling their language remains a significant hurdle. Our proposed model, PIDD, leverages prompt engineering to overcome this limitation. By incorporating a dual prompt framework, PIDD isolates image details and linguistic expressions, enabling direct manipulation of image description styles. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of PIDD in incorporating diverse image description styles and prompts, surpassing state-of-the-art models in image description tasks. Contemporary research into elastic actuators and quadruped robots is gaining momentum, driven by their complementary advantages in mobility and efficiency. When implemented in quadrupedal locomotion, these actuators offer increased power-to-weight ratios and energy-saving capabilities. Current approaches typically rely on pre-defined elastic actuator models, which are tailored to specific robotic configurations and may not adapt well to changes or unexpected disruptions. This could lead to reduced precision and increased vulnerability in various scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we developed a more adaptive solution. This paper introduces a control policy optimized for quadruped robots equipped with elastic actuators, allowing these systems to automatically adjust their actuator settings in response to changes in body mass, leg length, and actuator properties. Our elastic actuator model is similarly flexible, treating each actuator as a variable-damping system. By integrating the elastic actuator model into a whole-body controller, we identified an open-loop policy to manage the actuator settings in response to external modifications. Our results demonstrate that this policy remains effective across a wide range of parameters and various gait patterns. Moreover, this policy can be applied to different robotic designs using a single set of parameters, eliminating the need for separate tuning. We also compared our approach with a traditional strategy and demonstrated its superior performance in several key aspects, including increased mobility, reduced energy consumption, and greater robustness against unexpected disruptions.
